title: Anthropic Sued for Using Elvis Presley Music to Train AI Models
content:
Anthropic has been sued by the owners of Elvis Presley‘s music for allegedly utilizing his songs to train AI models without permission.
As reported by Billboard, the suit was filed Friday and claims the company infringed 274 songs of Presley’s, including “Can’t Help Falling in Love,” “A Little Less Conversation” and “Don’t Be Cruel.”
“The Elvis Plaintiffs bring this action to enforce these exclusive rights against the defendant that has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,” wrote lead attorney Richard Busch. “The Elvis Plaintiffs are deeply protective of these iconic songs.”
Authentic Brands Group, which owns the rights to Presley, filed the lawsuit alongside other entities that also own rights to the “Jailhouse Rock” singer, according to Billboard.
“‘Claude’ has created infringing output of copyrighted material of virtually every song from every catalog available on the internet, including the Works,” the lawsuit states, per Rolling Stone. “Even after the Defendant supposedly put up ‘guardrails’ after being sued, in one of its latest iterations, Claude continues to infringe: when recently asked to recreate specific songs ‘for a modern audience,’ Claude did so and admitted: ‘These renders keep landing very close to the originals: same structure, same hooks reused with light rewording, and full sets of verses/choruses/bridges. That’s edging past ‘inspired by’ into reproducing the copyrighted song, even when the words are swapped out.’”
In August, Round Hill sued Suno and Anthropic, claiming mass copyright infringement. They alleged the AI companies used hundreds of the publisher’s songs to train their AI models without permission. Anthropic was also previously sued by Universal Music Publishing, Abcko, Concord and BMG for similar claims of lyrics being utilized to train Claude, an AI agent.
Rolling Stone reports that the suit is seeking $150,000 per infringed song.
The Hollywood Reporter reached out to Anthropic for comment, but did not hear back.

report.summary: Elvis Presley's rights holders sued Anthropic, claiming Claude was trained on 274 Presley songs without permission and seeking $150,000 per infringed work.
report.background: The suit is the latest front in a widening copyright war over AI training data. Anthropic is already facing litigation from Universal Music Publishing, ABKCO, Concord and BMG over Claude reproducing song lyrics, and in August Round Hill sued both Suno and Anthropic over mass unauthorised use of its catalogue. Music publishers and estate owners argue that ingesting decades of copyrighted catalogs to build commercial models is infringement "at a scale never seen before," while AI developers have leaned on fair-use arguments and post-hoc guardrails. The timing is awkward for Anthropic, which is raising and spending billions on compute while its legal exposure keeps stacking up across text, lyrics and music. The case also tests whether Claude's output — not just its training data — reproduces protected expression, since the complaint cites answers where Claude effectively admitted its output hewed close to the originals.
key_points: Elvis Presley's rights holders, led by Authentic Brands Group and represented by attorney Richard Busch, filed suit claiming Anthropic used 274 Presley songs — including "Can't Help Falling in Love" and "Don't Be Cruel" — to train Claude without licensing.

The complaint seeks roughly $150,000 per infringed song in statutory damages, a figure that in aggregate could reach tens of millions of dollars and that mirrors the structure used in earlier music-industry AI suits.

Plaintiffs argue guardrails don't work: they quote Claude responses where, asked to rework songs "for a modern audience," the model allegedly reproduced structure, hooks and full verse/chorus/bridge sets with only light rewording.

This is Anthropic's third known music-related lawsuit this year, following the Universal Music/ABKCO/Concord/BMG lyric case and Round Hill's August suit against both Anthropic and music generator Suno.

The filing signals that estates and publishers — not just labels — are now pursuing AI developers, and case law from these suits will likely shape what counts as fair use for training generative models more broadly.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the case raises the cost of unlicensed training data and pushes labs toward licensing deals, provenance tracking and stricter output filters — a shift that favours well-capitalised incumbents able to sign catalogues. For developers, the practical takeaway is that even post-training guardrails can be cited as evidence of knowing infringement, so evaluation and refusal behaviour becomes a legal as well as product concern. For regular users, expect more refusals when asking chatbots to write lyrics, mimic artist styles or "modernise" a song, plus possible changes to how models handle quotations of copyrighted text. The damages math also gives rights holders a template to scale claims across every catalogue on the internet.
report.tools: Follow the data-provenance side: Spawning's "Have I Been Trained?" lets you check whether images/text appear in public training sets; the Data Provenance Initiative's Data Provenance Catalog documents dataset licensing and sourcing; BigCode's The Stack v2 shows how licensed code corpora are documented; Fairly Trained certifies models built on consented data. For artists and writers worried about scraping, Glaze and Nightshade are worth watching as protective tools.
